Tune Your Guitar by Ear

Pick a way to tune, then follow the steps one string at a time. The fretboard shows where to put your fingers; click any spot on it to hear that note. No guitar knowledge needed: strings are numbered 6 (the thickest, nearest your chin) to 1 (the thinnest), and frets are counted from the end where the tuning pegs are.

Your ear is the tuner. Every method here asks you to listen: to two notes agreeing, to a wobble slowing down, to a chord sounding sweet. The microphone reading is there to check your ear, not to replace it. With Ear first ticked it stays blurred until you've said what you hear. Start that habit today: musicians who only tune by looking at a screen can't hear when they've drifted out of tune halfway through a song.

1. Your guitar and how you'll tune it

Note names, or with octaves (C2 G2 C3 G3 C4 E4). Notes below about D2 are too low for the microphone reading.

3. Check your ear

What do you hear?

With speakers, the page's own reference and drone reach the microphone too: stop them, or use headphones, when you check. Keys: Space reference, ← → strings, d drone, m microphone.

Tips that apply to every method

  • Tune up to the note. If a string is sharp, go below the note and come back up. The string then holds its pitch better.
  • Turn while the string rings. Small turns. You hear the change happen.
  • Hum or sing the note. If you can sing the reference and then sing the string, your ear is doing the work.
  • Finish with a chord. Every method ends at your ear: strum something and adjust any string that sounds sour.
  • New strings stretch and go flat for a day or two. Tune, play, tune again.

Why there are several methods, and what each gets wrong: Tuning 1: your ear and beats, Tuning 2: fifth-fret, harmonics, octaves, Tuning 3: tuners and their limits. Something always out however you tune? The Setup Check finds out whether the guitar needs an adjustment.
